content: 1. Sim J and Dawson A explored the concept of informed consent in cluster-randomized trials, emphasizing the ethical complexities and challenges inherent in such research designs. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2012. 2. Weijer C, Grimshaw JM, Eccles MP, and colleagues developed the Ottawa Statement, which provides ethical guidelines for the design and conduct of cluster-randomized trials. This work was published in PLoS Medicine in 2012. 3. Löwy I examined the historical interplay between epidemiology, immunology, and yellow fever control efforts led by the Rockefeller Foundation in Brazil from 1923 to 1939. This analysis was published in the Journal of the History of Biology in 1997. 4. Boo CS discussed the legislative measures implemented in Singapore to control dengue, highlighting the role of policy in public health interventions. This was detailed in the Dengue Bulletin in 2001. 5. Teng AK and Singh S reviewed the epidemiology of dengue in Malaysia and outlined new initiatives for its prevention and control. Their work appeared in the Dengue Bulletin in 2001. 6. Viennet E, Ritchie SA, Williams CR, Faddy HM, and Harley D analyzed public health responses and challenges in controlling dengue transmission in high-income countries through four case studies. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. 7. Jamrozik E, Fuente-Núñez V, Reis A, Ringwald P, and Selgelid MJ addressed the ethical considerations in malaria control and research, emphasizing the need for ethical frameworks in global health. This was published in Malaria Journal in 2015. 8. Gimnig JE, Walker ED, Otieno P, and colleagues investigated the incidence of malaria among mosquito collectors conducting human landing catches in western Kenya. Their study was published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2013. 9. Achee NL, Youngblood L, Bangs MJ, Lavery JV, and James S provided a comprehensive tool for investigators and regulators to consider the ethical use of human participants in vector biology research. This was published in Vector-Borne and Zoonotic Diseases in 2015. 10. Lu F, Culleton R, Zhang M, and colleagues reported the emergence of indigenous artemisinin-resistant Plasmodium falciparum in Africa, raising significant concerns for malaria treatment. This was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2017. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided an epidemiological update on yellow fever on March 16, 2017, highlighting the ongoing challenges in controlling outbreaks. 12. Bambery B, Selgelid M, Weijer C, Savulescu J, and Pollard AJ proposed ethical criteria for conducting human challenge studies in infectious diseases, emphasizing the balance between scientific advancement and participant safety. This was published in Public Health Ethics in 2015. 13. Darton TC, Blohmke CJ, Moorthy VS, Altmann DM, Hayden FG, Clutterbuck EA, and colleagues discussed the design, recruitment, and microbiological considerations in human challenge studies. Their work appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2015. 14. The WHO published regulatory considerations for human challenge trials in vaccine development in 2016, providing guidance for ethical and scientific conduct. 15. Ethical considerations for Zika virus human challenge trials were outlined in a WHO report, emphasizing the importance of participant safety and public health benefits. 16. McGraw EA and O’Neill SL explored innovative approaches beyond insecticides to address vector-borne diseases, focusing on sustainable and effective solutions. This was published in Nature Reviews Microbiology in 2013. 17. Hoffmann AA, Montgomery BL, Popovici J, and colleagues demonstrated the successful establishment of Wolbachia in Aedes mosquito populations to suppress dengue transmission. This was published in Nature in 2011. 18. Jeffery JAL, Yen NT, Nam VS, Hoffmann AA, Kay BH, and Ryan PA characterized Aedes aegypti populations in a Vietnamese village to prepare for a Wolbachia-based mosquito control strategy aimed at eliminating dengue. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. 19. Chang MS, Christophel E-M, Gopinath D, and Abdur RM discussed the challenges and future perspectives for dengue vector control in the Western Pacific Region. This was published in the Western Pacific Surveillance and Response Journal in 2011. 20. The WHO outlined the Wolbachia-based mosquito suppression strategy as a promising tool for controlling dengue transmission, accessible through their public health research platform. 21. The WHO published a guidance framework in 2014 for testing genetically modified mosquitoes, addressing ethical, ecological, and public health considerations. 22. Hirsch F, Lévy Y, and Chneiweiss H presented a European perspective on genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR-Cas9, emphasizing responsible research practices. This was published in Nature in 2017. 23. Chneiweiss H, Hirsch F, Montoliu L, Müller AM, Fenet S, Abecassis M, and colleagues advocated for fostering responsible research with genome editing technologies, providing a European perspective. This was published in Transgenic Research in 2017. 24. The National Academy of Sciences published a report in 2016 on gene drives, addressing scientific advancements, uncertainties, and alignment with public values. 25. Pugh J examined the ethical implications of eradicating mosquitoes using gene-drive technologies, questioning the balance between ecological impact and public health benefits. This was published in the Journal of Medical Ethics in 2016. 26. The WHO convened a scoping meeting on February 23–24, 2017, to identify ethical issues associated with vector-borne diseases (VBDs). Over 25 international experts discussed key topics, including environmental and social determinants of health, ethics in vector control (including new technologies), surveillance and research ethics, and the ethics of mass public health interventions.
